items.method: Rule-by-rule elimination on an ordering game

steps.title: Name the game
steps.text: Five entities, five slots, one each — a pure ordering (sequencing) game. For a 'could be the order' question, you never need a full solve: each rule eliminates the answer choices that break it.

steps.title: Write out the elements
steps.text: List the roster and the board before touching the rules: associates F, G, H, J, K into slots 1–5. Writing the inventory first is what lets you see leftovers later.

representation.note: Empty board — inventory only. Slots run left to right, first to last.

steps.title: Symbolize each rule
steps.text: Turn every rule into notation you can scan in one glance. An 'immediately before' rule is a block; a fixed slot is an equation; a forbidden slot is a strike-out.

rules.note: A block: F and H are adjacent, F on the left. They move together.
Fixed placement — write J straight onto the board.
An exclusion — mark slot 1 with ~K.

steps.title: Sketch the board
steps.text: Put the fixed and forbidden marks on the board. J owns slot 4; slot 1 bars K. The [F H] block floats — it needs two adjacent open slots, so it must fit in 1–2, 2–3, or… not 4–5 (J blocks 4).

representation.note: The [F H] block can only occupy slots 1–2 or 2–3.

steps.title: Run each rule against the choices
steps.text: Take one rule at a time and cross off violators. Rule 1 [F H]: choice A splits F and H (F first, H third) and choice E reverses them — gone. Rule 2 J = 4: choice B puts J fifth — gone. Rule 3 K ≠ 1: choice C opens with K — gone. An elimination grid makes the sweep mechanical.

cells.note: F and H are not adjacent.

representation.note: Rows are answer choices; columns are rules. One 'no' kills a row.

steps.title: One choice survives
steps.text: Only D remains: F, H, K, J, G. Check it once — F immediately before H (slots 1–2), J fourth, K second (not first). Every rule holds, so D is correct.

items.method: Chain forced placements from a local condition

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If H argues third…' is a local question: it adds a temporary condition. Redraw the board with the new fact and chase every consequence before reading a single answer choice.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Same game, same notation. Keep the three rules in view — the new condition will interact with all of them.

steps.title: Place the condition
steps.text: Drop H into slot 3. The block [F H] instantly forces F into slot 2 — that is the whole point of symbolizing adjacency as a block. J was already fixed in slot 4.

representation.note: H = 3 (given) drags F to 2 via the [F H] block.

steps.title: Chase the leftovers
steps.text: Only G and K remain, and only slots 1 and 5 are open. K ≠ 1 forbids K from slot 1, so K takes 5 and G takes 1. The entire order is forced: G, F, H, J, K.

representation.note: Fully determined — a must-be-true question with one possible world.

steps.title: Match the forced board to the choices
steps.text: G argues first, so E must be true. The wrong answers contradict the forced board: F is second (not first, killing A), K is fifth (killing B and D), and J is fourth (killing C).

items.method: Block-and-order elimination on a six-slot sequence

steps.title: Write out the elements
steps.text: Six students — F, G, H, J, K, M — into slots 1 through 6, one each. Bigger board, same discipline: inventory first.

representation.note: Empty six-slot board.

steps.title: Symbolize: two blocks, two orderings
steps.text: Two adjacency blocks and two loose before/after rules. Note the difference in notation — a dash (K … M) allows any gap; a block [F G] allows none. Rule 4 chains the blocks: the [F G] block sits somewhere before the [H J] block.

rules.note: Adjacent, F left.
Adjacent, H left.

rules.rule_text: K argues at some time before M.
rules.note: Any gap allowed.

rules.rule_text: F argues at some time before H.
rules.note: Combining with the blocks: the F-G pair precedes the H-J pair.

steps.title: One rule at a time across the choices
steps.text: Rule 4 (F before H): choice A opens with H, J — dead. Rule 1 [F G]: choice C wedges K between F and G — dead. Rule 2 [H J]: choice D separates H (slot 3) from J (slot 5) — dead. Rule 3 K — M: choice E puts K sixth, after M — dead.

steps.title: Verify the survivor
steps.text: B — F, G, K, H, J, M — passes every rule: [F G] in 1–2, [H J] in 4–5, K (3) before M (6), F (1) before H (4). B is correct.

items.method: Abstract the argument's form, then match it

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: 'Most similar in its reasoning' is a parallel-reasoning question. The content (law firms, supreme courts) is a distraction — only the argument's skeleton matters. Extract the form before reading any choice.

steps.title: Map the argument
steps.text: Two premises feed one conclusion: a universal rule about a group, plus a membership claim placing Maria in the group.

nodes.text: Every senior partner has argued before the state supreme court.
Maria has argued before the state supreme court.

steps.title: Reduce to symbols
steps.text: Strip the content away entirely. This is universal instantiation — a valid form. Your job is now to find the choice with exactly this notation, and to reject choices whose notation differs.

rules.rule_text: Every senior partner has argued at the supreme court.
rules.note: P = senior partner, Q = has argued there.
Valid: universal instantiation.

steps.title: Match forms, not topics
steps.text: B swaps 'all' for 'most' — probabilistic, not universal. C runs the conditional backward (affirming the consequent: Q, therefore P). D does the same trick with an if-then. E reasons from a negative universal to a 'might' — no instantiation at all. Each fails on form, not subject matter.

steps.title: The matching skeleton
steps.text: A — all birds have feathers; a penguin is a bird; so a penguin has feathers — is 'All P are Q; x is P; ∴ x is Q' exactly. A is correct.

items.method: Find the causal leap, then supply the alternative cause

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A weaken question. First isolate the conclusion and the evidence; the gap between them is where the correct answer will strike.

steps.title: Map the argument
steps.text: The planner's evidence is a correlation across other cities; the conclusion is a causal prediction about this one. Notice the unstated assumption doing the real work.

nodes.text: Every comparable city that built light rail saw congestion fall within five years.
(Unstated) The rail line itself caused those congestion drops.
Building light rail here will reduce downtown congestion.

steps.title: Attack the assumption
steps.text: Correlation-to-causation arguments break when something else could explain the observed effect. To weaken, look for an answer that supplies a rival cause for the congestion drop in those comparable cities — not one that quibbles about cost, popularity, or engineering.

steps.title: Discard the off-point choices
steps.text: A (cost) changes the price, not the congestion logic. B (construction noise) is irrelevant to whether rail reduces traffic. C (rider satisfaction) mildly supports the planner. E (underground routing) says nothing about the causal claim. None touches the assumption.

steps.title: The rival cause
steps.text: D reveals that every comparable city also enacted congestion-pricing tolls — a confound that could explain the entire congestion drop without the rail line. That severs evidence from conclusion, so D most weakens the argument.

items.method: Symbolize the conditional, apply the contrapositive

steps.title: Spot the conditional
steps.text: One if-then plus one fact. Any 'properly concluded' question over a conditional is asking whether you can run modus ponens or modus tollens — and only those. Symbolize before judging any choice.

steps.title: Write the rule and its contrapositive
steps.text: Translate the sentence into arrow notation, then write the contrapositive immediately — on the LSAT the contrapositive is usually the version you will actually use.

rules.rule_text: If the contract is enforceable, then it was signed by both parties.
rules.note: E = enforceable, S = signed by both.
Flip and negate both sides.

rules.rule_text: The contract was not signed by both parties.
rules.note: The given fact — it matches the contrapositive's trigger.

steps.title: Fire the contrapositive
steps.text: ¬S is exactly the left side of ¬S → ¬E, so ¬E follows: the contract is not enforceable. This is modus tollens. Note what you may NOT do: from E → S alone, knowing S would prove nothing about E (that would be affirming the consequent).

steps.title: Test each choice against ¬E
steps.text: A asserts E — the direct opposite of the valid inference. C invents 'partially enforceable', a category the stimulus never defines. D adds facts about intent that appear nowhere. E denies that a conclusion exists when modus tollens plainly yields one.

steps.title: The valid conclusion
steps.text: B — the contract is not enforceable — is exactly ¬E, the modus tollens conclusion. B is correct.

items.method: Map the passage's structure, then match the thesis

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: Main-point questions reward structure over detail. Before evaluating choices, reconstruct what each paragraph does — the thesis is usually the through-line, not any single sentence.

steps.title: Map the paragraphs
steps.text: Four paragraphs, one arc: problem → failed fix → deliberate solution → modern contest. The load-bearing move is in paragraph 3: the drafters knowingly traded predictability for access.

paragraphs.gist: Writ-system pleading punished procedural missteps; the Field Code was a partial remedy.
Fact pleading bred its own pathologies; Clark's generation urged mere fair notice.
The 1938 Rules deliberately traded doctrinal predictability for procedural access; Conley cemented it.
Twombly/Iqbal's plausibility threshold — defenders and critics contest whether the bargain is being unwound.

steps.title: State the main point in your own words
steps.text: Something like: the move from rigid pleading to notice pleading was a conscious trade — predictability sacrificed for access — and that bargain is still contested. Now hunt for the choice that captures BOTH halves of the trade.

steps.title: Discard the overreaches
steps.text: A says courts 'always' preferred bright-line rules — extreme and unsupported. B claims all barriers were eliminated — paragraph 4 contradicts it. C says drafters 'rejected' the common-law tradition — too strong; they were informed by it. D equates Twombly/Iqbal with full nineteenth-century restoration — the passage says only 'partial'.

steps.title: The choice with both halves
steps.text: E — the shift reflected a deliberate trade of doctrinal predictability for procedural access — matches the paragraph-3 thesis and the arc of the whole map. E is correct.

items.method: Locate, verify, and beware neighboring dates

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: 'According to the passage' plus a specific fact = a detail question. Do not answer from memory — locate the line, because detail questions bait you with other numbers that appear nearby in the text.

steps.title: Know where facts live
steps.text: Your paragraph map says dates and rule history live in paragraph 3 (adoption era) and paragraph 4 (modern cases). Go to paragraph 3 for the Rules' effective date.

paragraphs.gist: Fact pleading's pathologies; Clark's notice-pleading idea.
Original Federal Rules take effect; Rule 8(a)(2); Conley v. Gibson (1957).

steps.title: Disarm the decoys
steps.text: 1848 belongs to the Field Code (paragraph 1) — and 1948 echoes it. 1957 is Conley v. Gibson, the case that later cemented the standard. 1966 and 1975 appear nowhere in the passage. Every decoy is a real number from the wrong sentence.

steps.title: Read the line itself
steps.text: Paragraph 3 states the original Federal Rules 'took effect in 1938.' A is correct.

items.method: Ask what work the detail does for the author

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: 'Primarily in order to' asks for the detail's FUNCTION, not its content. The answer describes what the mention accomplishes in the author's structure — so the structure map, not the sentence alone, decides it.

steps.title: Place the detail in the arc
steps.text: The Field Code appears at the hinge between paragraph 1 (problem) and paragraph 2 (the fix's own failure). It is introduced as a 'partial remedy' — and the very next paragraph opens with fact pleading generating 'its own pathologies'.

paragraphs.gist: Writ system punishes missteps; Field Code of 1848 offered a partial remedy (fact pleading).
Fact pleading generated its own pathologies — setting up the notice-pleading idea.

steps.title: Phrase the function yourself
steps.text: The Field Code's job in the passage: show an early reform that fixed part of the problem but created new ones — a stepping stone that motivates the next reform. Look for a choice saying exactly that, at that temperature.

steps.title: Discard the wrong temperatures
steps.text: A reverses the author's stance (nothing says fact pleading beat notice pleading). C inflates one example into a leadership claim. D contradicts the passage — the writ system WAS replaced. E turns one bumpy reform into 'reform inevitably fails', far beyond the author's measured tone.

steps.title: The matching function
steps.text: B — illustrate an early reform effort that solved some problems but introduced new ones — is precisely the stepping-stone role the map shows. B is correct.

items.method: Chain forced placements from a local condition

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If G argues fifth…' is a local question. Redraw the board with G in slot 5 and chase every consequence before touching the choices.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Same game, same notation — keep all three rules in view.

rules.note: Adjacent block, F left.
Fixed — write it on the board.
Mark slot 1 with ~K.

steps.title: Place the condition
steps.text: Put G in slot 5. J was already fixed in slot 4. That leaves slots 1, 2, and 3 for F, H, and K — and the [F H] block needs two of them, adjacent.

representation.note: Only slots 1–3 remain open, and [F H] must fit inside them.

steps.title: Chase the leftovers
steps.text: The [F H] block can sit in 1–2 or 2–3. If it took 2–3, K would be forced into slot 1 — forbidden by K ≠ 1. So the block takes 1–2, and K takes the only seat left, slot 3. The whole order is forced: F, H, K, J, G.

representation.note: One possible world — a must-be-true question with a fully forced board.

steps.title: Match the forced board
steps.text: K argues third, so A must be true. The wrong answers contradict the forced order: H is second, F is first, J is fourth, and K ≠ 1 already barred K from opening.

items.method: Enumerate the valid worlds, then test the extremes

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'CANNOT be true' is a global question: the right answer fails in every valid order, and each wrong answer succeeds in at least one. When a game is small, listing the valid orders outright is the fastest weapon.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Three rules, five slots — this game is tightly constrained, so a full enumeration will be short.

rules.note: Adjacent block, F left.
Fixed — write it on the board.
Mark slot 1 with ~K.

steps.title: Where can the [F H] block go?
steps.text: J owns slot 4, so the block cannot use 3–4 or 4–5. That leaves [F H] in slots 1–2 or 2–3. Everything else follows from that split.

representation.note: Block windows: 1–2 or 2–3. Note what that does to H — it can only ever sit in slot 2 or slot 3.

steps.title: List every valid order
steps.text: Block in 1–2: G and K fill 3 and 5 in either order — two worlds. Block in 2–3: K ≠ 1 forces G into slot 1 and K into slot 5 — one world. Three valid orders total.

steps.title: Test the choices against the three worlds
steps.text: H sits in slot 2 or 3 in every world, so 'H argues first' can never happen — B cannot be true. Each other choice occurs somewhere: K fifth (world 1), G third (world 2), F second (world 3), K third (world 1).

items.method: Chain forced placements from a local condition

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If K argues third…' is a local question: add the condition to the board and push the rules until nothing else moves.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Keep the three rules in front of you — the block is the engine here.

rules.note: Adjacent block, F left.
Fixed — write it on the board.
Mark slot 1 with ~K.

steps.title: Place the condition
steps.text: K takes slot 3 and J was already fixed in slot 4. Now ask: where can the [F H] block still fit? It needs two adjacent open slots.

representation.note: Open slots: 1, 2, 5. The only adjacent pair is 1–2.

steps.title: The block has one home
steps.text: Slots 1–2 are the only adjacent open pair, so F takes 1 and H takes 2. G inherits the last seat, slot 5. The order is fully forced: F, H, K, J, G.

representation.note: Fully determined — exactly one world satisfies the condition.

steps.title: Match the forced board
steps.text: G argues fifth, so C must be true. Against the forced order the others fail: H is second (not first, not fourth), F is first (not second), and G is fifth (not first).

items.method: Find the hidden parity constraint

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'Each could be true EXCEPT' means four choices happen in some valid order and one never does. Look for a structural constraint — often a slot an entity can never occupy.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Two adjacency blocks plus two ordering rules. Blocks eat pairs of consecutive slots — that geometry is the key.

rules.note: Adjacent, F left.
Adjacent, H left.

rules.rule_text: K argues at some time before M.
rules.note: Any gap allowed.

rules.rule_text: F argues at some time before H.
rules.note: The F-G block sits somewhere before the H-J block.

steps.title: Watch what the blocks do to M
steps.text: The two blocks [F G] and [H J] occupy two disjoint pairs of consecutive slots, and K precedes M. Try to build any valid order and track where M lands: the blocks tile the row so tightly that K and M are forced into the leftover pair of slots, with M after K.

representation.note: Six slots, two 2-slot blocks, and the K–M pair: three 'units' of width 2 filling the row.

steps.title: M's possible seats
steps.text: Treat [F G], [H J], and (K…M) as three width-2 units. However you arrange them, M sits at the right edge of its unit — an even slot. Enumerate: M can testify second, fourth, or sixth, never in an odd slot.

rules.symbols: K M | F G | H J  →  M = 2
F G | K M | H J  →  M = 4
F G | H J | K M  →  M = 6

steps.title: Apply the parity fact
steps.text: M can never argue third — an odd slot — so D is the exception. The rest all occur: F first and G second in most worlds, H fourth in F-G-K-H-J-M, K fifth in F-G-H-J-K-M.

items.method: Chain forced placements from a local condition

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If K argues fifth…' is a local question. Place K, then let the ordering rules squeeze everything else.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Two blocks and two ordering rules — note the derived rule: the F-G block precedes the H-J block.

rules.note: Adjacent, F left.
Adjacent, H left.

rules.rule_text: K argues at some time before M.
rules.note: Any gap allowed.

rules.rule_text: F argues at some time before H.
rules.note: The F-G block sits somewhere before the H-J block.

steps.title: Place the condition and push K — M
steps.text: K in slot 5 leaves only slot 6 after it, so M must be sixth. Slots 1–4 are now exactly four seats for the two blocks.

representation.note: Blocks [F G] and [H J] must tile slots 1–4.

steps.title: Order the blocks
steps.text: F argues before H, so the F-G block takes 1–2 and the H-J block takes 3–4. The full order is forced: F, G, H, J, K, M.

representation.note: One world — every seat is decided.

steps.title: Match the forced board
steps.text: H argues third, so C must be true. Against the forced order: F is first, G is second, J is fourth, and M is sixth — each wrong choice contradicts a forced seat.

items.method: Test the block's remaining windows

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If K argues third…' is a local question. K in slot 3 splits the row and shrinks the windows where each block can fit — test them.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: The derived rule matters again: [F G] must finish before [H J] begins.

rules.note: Adjacent, F left.
Adjacent, H left.

rules.rule_text: K argues at some time before M.
rules.note: Any gap allowed.

rules.rule_text: F argues at some time before H.
rules.note: The F-G block sits somewhere before the H-J block.

steps.title: Place the condition
steps.text: K takes slot 3. The [F G] block now needs two adjacent open slots: the candidates are 1–2, 4–5, and 5–6.

representation.note: Where can [F G] still fit? Test each window against F — H.

steps.title: Kill the late windows
steps.text: If [F G] sat in 4–5 or 5–6, then H — which must come after F with the whole [H J] block behind it — would have at most one slot left. Impossible. So [F G] takes 1–2: F first, G second. The two survivors are F-G-K-H-J-M and F-G-K-M-H-J.

representation.note: Slots 4–6 hold [H J] and M, in either arrangement that keeps K before M.

steps.title: Find what holds in both worlds
steps.text: F argues first in both surviving orders, so E must be true. The other placements each hold in only one of the two worlds — H fourth, M sixth, and J fifth only in the first; H fifth only in the second.

items.method: Derive a relational fact from the blocks

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: A global 'must be true' with relational choices (X before Y). Don't enumerate every order — derive the relationship directly from the rules.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Focus on how [F G] interacts with F — H.

rules.note: Adjacent, F left.
Adjacent, H left.

rules.rule_text: K argues at some time before M.
rules.note: Any gap allowed.

rules.rule_text: F argues at some time before H.
rules.note: The F-G block sits somewhere before the H-J block.

steps.title: Chain the two rules
steps.text: G sits in the slot immediately after F. H comes after F too — but H cannot take G's slot (G is there). So H is at least two slots after F, which puts H after G in every valid order.

rules.rule_text: G's seat is pinned to F's.

rules.note: G always testifies before H — a derived rule the choices will probe.

steps.title: Apply the derived rule
steps.text: G argues before H in every valid order, so B must be true. Each other relational claim fails somewhere: K can follow F (F-G-H-J-K-M), H can follow K (F-G-K-H-J-M), K can lead (K-F-G-H-J-M puts K before F), and M can precede J (F-G-K-M-H-J).

items.method: Rule-by-rule elimination on an ordering game

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: An 'acceptable order' question: no solving needed. Take one rule at a time and cross off every choice that breaks it — exactly one will survive.

steps.title: Write out the elements
steps.text: Six witnesses — L, M, N, P, R, T — into sessions 1 through 6. T is already pinned to session 4 and L is restricted to the edges.

representation.note: L may only take session 1 or 6.

steps.title: Symbolize each rule
steps.text: Four rules: a block, a loose ordering, a fixed seat, and an either/or edge rule.

rules.note: Adjacent block, M left.

rules.rule_text: N testifies at some time before R.
rules.note: Any gap allowed.
Fixed — the board's anchor.
L brackets the schedule — split into two worlds.

steps.title: Sweep the choices one rule at a time
steps.text: Apply [M P] first, then N — R, then T = 4, then the L edge rule. Each rule knocks out at least one listed order; keep a tally rather than re-checking whole orders.

steps.title: The survivor
steps.text: N, M, P, T, R, L passes every rule — M immediately before P (sessions 2–3), N (1) before R (5), T fourth, L sixth — so C is correct. The others each break exactly one rule: a split M/P pair, R before N, T in the wrong session, or L stuck in the middle.

items.method: Enumerate the worlds, then test the negative claim

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: A global 'must be true'. With T fixed and L restricted to the edges, this game has very few valid orders — enumerate them once and answer every global question from the list.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: T = 4 anchors the middle; L = 1 ∨ 6 splits the game into two worlds to explore.

rules.note: Adjacent block, M left.

rules.rule_text: N testifies at some time before R.
rules.note: Any gap allowed.
Fixed — the board's anchor.
L brackets the schedule — split into two worlds.

steps.title: Build the four valid orders
steps.text: In each L-world, the [M P] block has exactly two homes, and N — R fills what remains. That yields four orders in total.

rules.symbols: M P N T R L
N M P T R L
L M P T N R
L N R T M P

steps.title: Look at session 1 across all four
steps.text: The first session is always M, N, or L. R never leads — it always needs N somewhere before it, and the surviving layouts put R in session 3, 5, or 6.

representation.note: R is barred from session 1 in every valid world.

steps.title: Match against the choices
steps.text: R never testifies first, so A must be true. Every other claim fails in at least one order: L sixth (not first) in two worlds, N floats between sessions 1, 2, 3 and 5, P can land second or third, and M leads only one world.

items.method: Split into the two surviving worlds

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If L testifies first…' is a local question that halves the game. Build both surviving worlds fully — the answer must hold in each.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: With L pinned to session 1, only the [M P] block placement still varies.

rules.note: Adjacent block, M left.

rules.rule_text: N testifies at some time before R.
rules.note: Any gap allowed.
Fixed — the board's anchor.
L brackets the schedule — split into two worlds.

steps.title: Place the condition
steps.text: L first, T fourth. The open seats are 2, 3, 5, 6, and the [M P] block needs an adjacent pair: 2–3 or 5–6.

representation.note: Two block windows → two worlds to build.

steps.title: Build both worlds
steps.text: Block in 2–3: N and R take 5 and 6 with N first → L, M, P, T, N, R. Block in 5–6: N and R take 2 and 3 with N first → L, N, R, T, M, P. Compare the two: in both, N sits in the session immediately before R.

rules.symbols: L M P T N R
rules.note: N fifth, R sixth — adjacent.

rules.symbols: L N R T M P
rules.note: N second, R third — adjacent.

steps.title: Find the invariant
steps.text: N testifies immediately before R in both worlds, so E must be true. The other claims each hold in only one world — M second, P third, R sixth in the first; and M before N fails outright in the second, where N is second and M fifth.

items.method: Test a disjunctive claim across every world

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: A global 'must be true' whose choices include an either/or. Disjunctions are weaker claims — easier to make true everywhere — so expect the credited answer to be one. Enumerate the worlds first.

steps.title: Recall the symbolized rules
steps.text: Same anchors: T = 4, L on an edge, [M P] block, N — R.

rules.note: Adjacent block, M left.

rules.rule_text: N testifies at some time before R.
rules.note: Any gap allowed.
Fixed — the board's anchor.
L brackets the schedule — split into two worlds.

steps.title: The four valid orders
steps.text: Two L-worlds times two block windows gives four orders. Write them down once.

rules.symbols: M P N T R L
N M P T R L
L M P T N R
L N R T M P

steps.title: Track R's predecessors
steps.text: In the first three orders M testifies before R. The fourth order (L, N, R, T, M, P) breaks that — M comes after R — but there L leads, so L precedes R instead. In every world, at least one of M and L is before R.

steps.title: Match the disjunction
steps.text: 'M before R, or L before R' survives all four orders, so C must be true. The stronger single claims each die in the fourth order — M and P both follow R there — while the remaining choices fail elsewhere: N can follow T, and T can follow R.

items.method: Rule-by-rule elimination on a selection game

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: An 'acceptable list' question on an in/out selection game. No deductions needed — run each conditional rule against the five listed rosters and cross off violators.

steps.title: Symbolize each conditional with its contrapositive
steps.text: Selection games live and die on conditionals. Write each rule as an arrow AND flip it — the contrapositive is what usually does the eliminating.

rules.rule_text: If F is displayed, then H is displayed.
rules.note: Write every conditional with its contrapositive.

rules.rule_text: If G is displayed, then K is not displayed.
rules.note: G and K can never both be in.

rules.rule_text: If H is displayed, then J is not displayed.
rules.note: H and J can never both be in.

rules.rule_text: Exactly three of the six are displayed.
rules.note: A selection (in/out) game, not an ordering game.

steps.title: Sweep the choices one rule at a time
steps.text: Rule 1 (F → H): cross off any roster showing F without H. Rule 2 (G → ¬K): cross off any roster with both G and K. Rule 3 (H → ¬J): cross off any roster with both H and J. Count what falls to each.

steps.title: The survivor
steps.text: G, H, and L is the only roster that violates nothing: no F (Rule 1 idle), G in with K out, H in with J out — so B is correct. Two choices pair F without H, one pairs G with K, and one pairs H with J.

items.method: Read incompatibility straight off a conditional

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'CANNOT both be displayed' asks for a forbidden pair. A rule of the form X → ¬Y bans the pair {X, Y} outright — check the rules before testing anything by hand.

steps.title: Symbolize each conditional with its contrapositive
steps.text: Two of the three rules are direct incompatibilities; the F rule is a requirement, not a ban.

rules.rule_text: If F is displayed, then H is displayed.
rules.note: Write every conditional with its contrapositive.

rules.rule_text: If G is displayed, then K is not displayed.
rules.note: G and K can never both be in.

rules.rule_text: If H is displayed, then J is not displayed.
rules.note: H and J can never both be in.

rules.rule_text: Exactly three of the six are displayed.
rules.note: A selection (in/out) game, not an ordering game.

steps.title: Which pairs do the rules actually forbid?
steps.text: G → ¬K bans {G, K}. H → ¬J bans {H, J}. Nothing else is banned by a single rule — F → H permits F and H together (in fact it demands H when F is in). Any pair not on the banned list can usually be realized in some legal roster.

cells.note: Free agent — no rule touches L.

representation.note: Forbidden pairs from the arrows: {G,K} and {H,J}.

steps.title: Match the banned pair to the choices
steps.text: G and K can never both hang — Rule 2 says so directly — making D the credited pair. Each other pair co-exists in a legal roster: F with H in {F,G,H}, H with L in {F,H,L}, J with L in {G,J,L}, K with L in {H,K,L}.

items.method: Fire the contrapositives, then count the seats

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If J is displayed…' is a local question on a selection game. Fire every contrapositive the condition triggers, then check who is left to fill the remaining seats.

steps.title: Symbolize each conditional with its contrapositive
steps.text: You will use the flipped forms here, not the originals.

rules.rule_text: If F is displayed, then H is displayed.
rules.note: Write every conditional with its contrapositive.

rules.rule_text: If G is displayed, then K is not displayed.
rules.note: G and K can never both be in.

rules.rule_text: If H is displayed, then J is not displayed.
rules.note: H and J can never both be in.

rules.rule_text: Exactly three of the six are displayed.
rules.note: A selection (in/out) game, not an ordering game.

steps.title: Chain from J in
steps.text: J in fires J → ¬H: H is out. H out fires ¬H → ¬F: F is out. Two of the three display seats remain, and only G, K, and L are still eligible.

representation.note: Two open seats, three candidates — and one pair of them is banned.

steps.title: Count the ways to fill two seats
steps.text: The two remaining seats come from {G, K, L}, but G and K cannot sit together (Rule 2). The only legal pairs are {G, L} and {K, L}. Notice what both have in common.

steps.title: The common member
steps.text: Both legal completions include L, so 'L is displayed' — choice A — must be true. G and K each appear in only one completion, and F and H were knocked out by the contrapositive chain before the seats were even counted.

items.method: Follow the forced chain from the supposition

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'Assuming F is displayed, each could also be displayed EXCEPT' — fire F's consequences first; the exception will be whoever those consequences lock out.

steps.title: Symbolize each conditional with its contrapositive
steps.text: F is the trigger of Rule 1 — start the chain there.

rules.rule_text: If F is displayed, then H is displayed.
rules.note: Write every conditional with its contrapositive.

rules.rule_text: If G is displayed, then K is not displayed.
rules.note: G and K can never both be in.

rules.rule_text: If H is displayed, then J is not displayed.
rules.note: H and J can never both be in.

rules.rule_text: Exactly three of the six are displayed.
rules.note: A selection (in/out) game, not an ordering game.

steps.title: Chain from F in
steps.text: F in fires F → H: H is displayed. H in fires H → ¬J: J is out. One display seat remains for G, K, or L (G and K still cannot pair, but only one seat is open anyway).

representation.note: The chain F ⇒ H ⇒ ¬J runs before any choice is read.

steps.title: The locked-out painting
steps.text: J can never join F — the chain F → H → ¬J bars it — so C is the exception. Each remaining painting fills the third seat in some legal roster: G in {F,G,H}, K in {F,H,K}, L in {F,H,L}, and H is displayed in all of them.

items.method: Prove a disjunction by contradiction

steps.title: Read the question type
steps.text: 'If K is not displayed…' is a local question, and one choice is a disjunction ('at least one of…'). The standard proof: suppose the disjunction fails and show the rules collapse.

steps.title: Symbolize each conditional with its contrapositive
steps.text: Keep the contrapositive of Rule 1 in view — it delivers the contradiction.

rules.rule_text: If F is displayed, then H is displayed.
rules.note: Write every conditional with its contrapositive.

rules.rule_text: If G is displayed, then K is not displayed.
rules.note: G and K can never both be in.

rules.rule_text: If H is displayed, then J is not displayed.
rules.note: H and J can never both be in.

rules.rule_text: Exactly three of the six are displayed.
rules.note: A selection (in/out) game, not an ordering game.

steps.title: Suppose H and J are BOTH out
steps.text: With K also out, three of the six paintings are gone, so the display would have to be exactly the remaining three: F, G, and L. But F displayed fires F → H, and H is out — contradiction. The supposition dies.

cells.note: Forced in… but F → H fails!

representation.note: Three exclusions force the other three in — and the forced roster breaks Rule 1.

steps.title: State what the contradiction proves
steps.text: H and J cannot both sit out when K is out, so at least one of them is displayed — D must be true. The single-painting claims all fail in some legal world: no F in {G,H,L}, no G in {F,H,L}, no L in {F,G,H}, and no H in {G,J,L}, where J carries the disjunct.

items.method: Name the term-shift between evidence and conclusion

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A flaw question ('most vulnerable to the criticism'). Before reading the choices, pin down exactly what the critics claimed and exactly what the editor's evidence measures — flaw answers usually live in the gap between two near-synonyms.

steps.title: Map the exchange
steps.text: The critics' claim and the editor's rebuttal are talking past each other. Put each on the board and label what each one is actually about.

nodes.text: Critics: the policy will reduce the DIVERSITY OF VIEWPOINTS we publish.
Editor: the SUBMISSION RATE has not dropped since the policy took effect.
Editor: so the critics are mistaken.

steps.title: Spot the switched measure
steps.text: The critics predicted a drop in one quantity (variety of viewpoints); the editor rebuts with a different quantity (number of submissions). The same pile of submissions could shrink in variety while holding steady in volume — the rebuttal never touches the critics' actual claim. That mismatch of terms is the flaw to find in the choices.

rules.note: Equivocation between two different measures.

steps.title: Match the flaw
steps.text: E states it exactly: the editor confuses the volume of submissions with the diversity of viewpoints within them. A and D describe conditional and sampling errors the argument never makes, B overstates the critics' premise, and C is a harmless side fact.

items.method: Find the causal leap, then name it

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A flaw question over a causal claim. When the evidence is a comparison between two groups and the conclusion says 'X causes Y', ask what ELSE could differ between the groups.

steps.title: Map the argument
steps.text: One correlational premise carries the whole causal conclusion — with an unstated assumption doing the real work.

nodes.text: Breakfast-eaters outperform breakfast-skippers on morning cognitive tests.
(Unstated) Nothing else about breakfast-eaters explains their scores.
Eating breakfast CAUSES improved cognitive performance.

steps.title: Generate rival explanations
steps.text: People who eat breakfast may also sleep more regularly, exercise, or differ in a dozen other ways — any of which could drive the test scores. The argument moves from 'correlated' to 'causes' without ruling any of these out. Look for the choice that names that move, not a peripheral quibble.

steps.title: Match the flaw
steps.text: C says it directly: the argument infers causation from correlation without ruling out alternative explanations. A, B, D, and E each poke at side issues — representativeness, definitions, test variety, exceptions — none of which is the load-bearing error.

items.method: Absence of evidence vs. evidence of absence

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A flaw question. Watch what the columnist's premise actually establishes: not that the supporters are wrong — only that they haven't documented their claim.

steps.title: Map the argument
steps.text: Notice the strength mismatch between premise and conclusion.

nodes.text: Supporters have produced NO architectural surveys backing their preservation claim.
Therefore the ordinance WILL NOT preserve the historic character.

steps.title: Name the pattern
steps.text: From 'the claim is unproven' the columnist concludes 'the claim is false.' But an undocumented claim can still be true — the ordinance's actual effect is untouched by whether anyone filed a survey. Arguing from a lack of evidence to the falsity of a claim is the appeal-to-ignorance pattern.

rules.note: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

steps.title: Match the flaw
steps.text: D — treating absence of evidence as evidence of absence — is exactly the move. A (circularity), B (small sample), C (division), and E (popularity) describe fallacies the columnist never commits.

items.method: Find what makes an elimination argument airtight

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: 'Depends on which assumption' is a NECESSARY-assumption question: the credited answer is something the argument cannot live without. Test candidates by negating them — if the negation wrecks the argument, you've found it.

steps.title: Symbolize the lawyer's logic
steps.text: The lawyer lists two routes to a win, eliminates one, and concludes the other must be the route.

rules.rule_text: To win, show misapplication or improper instruction.
rules.note: M = statute misapplied, I = jury improperly instructed.
Eliminate M from the disjunction… if the list was complete.

steps.title: Probe the hidden premise
steps.text: The elimination only goes through if M and I were the ONLY grounds for winning. Negate that: suppose some third ground existed — then a win would no longer guarantee improper instructions, and the conclusion collapses. That exhaustiveness is what the argument depends on.

steps.title: Match the assumption
steps.text: A — there are no other grounds on which the appeal could be won — is the necessary assumption. B and D assert outcomes the argument never needs, C confuses sufficiency with the stated necessity, and E is idle commentary about which ground was stronger.

items.method: Strengthen a causal claim by protecting the comparison

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A strengthen question. First find the argument's weakest joint; the credited answer will brace exactly that joint, not add applause.

steps.title: Map the argument
steps.text: A group comparison feeding a causal conclusion — the classic setup where group comparability is the hidden load-bearing wall.

nodes.text: Patients on the new therapy recovered faster than patients on the standard treatment.
(Unstated) The two groups were alike apart from the therapy.
The new therapy is more effective.

steps.title: Attack yourself, then defend
steps.text: The obvious rival story: the new-therapy patients were simply younger or healthier to begin with. A strengthener that closes THAT door — showing the groups matched on age, health, and severity — converts the raw comparison into real evidence of effectiveness. Cost, seniority, and side effects don't touch the causal joint.

steps.title: Match the strengthener
steps.text: C — the groups were similar in age, overall health, and severity — rules out the selection story and most strengthens the argument. A and E are about cost and side effects, D is an appeal to the researcher's résumé, and B if anything muddies the comparison.

items.method: Translate 'only', then chain the contrapositive

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A must-be-true question over two quantified statements. 'Only X may do Y' is the classic trap wording — translate it into an arrow before judging anything.

steps.title: Translate both statements
steps.text: 'Only employees who completed the course may operate' makes completion a REQUIREMENT of operating — the arrow starts at 'operate'.

rules.note: 'Only' introduces the necessary condition.
Always write it — it's usually the working form.

rules.rule_text: No temporary worker completed the course.

steps.title: Chain the arrows
steps.text: Link the second premise into the contrapositive: temp → ¬completed → ¬operate. Every temporary worker is barred from the forklift. Note what you may NOT infer: completion being necessary doesn't make it sufficient, so nothing follows about who DOES operate.

steps.title: Match the conclusion
steps.text: E — no temporary worker may operate the forklift — is the chained result. A contradicts it, B and D read the necessary condition as sufficient, and C reverses the first conditional.

items.method: Check which way the arrow was fired

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A flaw question over a conditional. Symbolize the rule, then check whether the critic argued WITH the arrow (valid) or AGAINST it (flaw).

steps.title: Symbolize the critic's argument
steps.text: Lay the rule and the observation side by side and watch the direction of inference.

rules.rule_text: If a film is a commercial success, it will be widely imitated.
The comedy has spawned a dozen imitators.
rules.note: The CONSEQUENT is what was observed.
The critic drove backwards up the arrow.

steps.title: Name the pattern
steps.text: From success → imitated plus 'imitated', nothing follows — imitation could have other causes (a striking style, a cheap formula). Concluding 'success' from the consequent is affirming the consequent. Contrast the valid forms: modus ponens fires on the ANTECEDENT; modus tollens fires on the NEGATED consequent.

steps.title: Match the flaw
steps.text: B captures it: the critic treats a result that success would produce as if it established success. A describes the necessary/sufficient confusion run the other way, and C, D, and E raise sampling, generalization, and merit issues that aren't the operative error.

items.method: Build the bridge premise

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: 'Follows logically if assumed' is a SUFFICIENT-assumption question: find the missing premise that makes the argument deductively valid. Mechanically: symbolize the rule and the conclusion, and see what bridges them.

steps.title: Lay out what's given and what's wanted
steps.text: One universal rule, one conclusion about Dana — the gap is glaring once symbolized.

rules.rule_text: Anyone who understands the proof will pass.

rules.note: What single fact would let the rule fire on Dana?

steps.title: Fire the rule on Dana
steps.text: The rule fires only when its antecedent holds. Feed it 'Dana understands the proof' and modus ponens delivers the conclusion outright. Anything probabilistic ('most'), reversed (pass → understand), or off-trigger (study habits) fails to guarantee it.

steps.title: Match the bridge
steps.text: A — Dana understands the proof — completes the deduction. B is off-trigger, D is merely probable, and C and E reverse the conditional, which never licenses the inference.

items.method: Chain the conditionals, then fire modus ponens

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A must-be-true question with two linked conditionals and one fact. Chain first, fire second.

steps.title: Symbolize and link
steps.text: The consequent of the first rule is the antecedent of the second — they weld into one long arrow.

rules.rule_text: If the witness is credible, the alibi holds.
If the alibi holds, the defendant was not at the scene.

rules.note: One arrow from credibility to absence from the scene.
The witness is credible.

steps.title: Fire the chain
steps.text: The given fact is the chain's trigger: C fires C → A (the alibi holds), which fires A → ¬S. Both intermediate and final links are now established — the defendant was not at the scene.

steps.title: Match the conclusion
steps.text: A — the defendant was not at the scene — is the chained modus ponens result. B and C contradict premises, E contradicts the valid conclusion, and D reverses the chain, which is never licensed.

items.method: Symbolize the rule, then fire modus ponens

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A 'properly concluded' question over one conditional and one fact. The only valid moves are modus ponens (the fact matches the antecedent) and modus tollens (the fact negates the consequent) — symbolize and check which applies.

steps.title: Translate the rule and the fact
steps.text: Write the arrow, its contrapositive, and the given fact — then compare the fact against the arrow's left side.

rules.rule_text: Impeachment with a prior inconsistent statement calls credibility into question.

rules.note: Valid to infer; the converse (Q → P) and inverse (¬P → ¬Q) are NOT.

rules.rule_text: Officer Reyes was impeached with a prior inconsistent statement.
rules.note: This matches the antecedent — modus ponens territory.

steps.title: Fire the rule
steps.text: The fact satisfies the antecedent exactly, so the consequent follows with certainty: Officer Reyes's credibility has been called into question. Watch the standard traps in the choices: the converse (treating the consequent as proof of the antecedent), the inverse (denying the antecedent), and out-of-scope add-ons the stimulus never mentions.

steps.title: Match the conclusion
steps.text: B is the modus ponens conclusion. A adds evidentiary exclusion the stimulus never mentions, C is the converse, D is the inverse, and E denies a conclusion the rule settles outright.

items.method: Symbolize the rule, then fire modus ponens

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A 'properly concluded' question over one conditional and one fact. The only valid moves are modus ponens (the fact matches the antecedent) and modus tollens (the fact negates the consequent) — symbolize and check which applies.

steps.title: Translate the rule and the fact
steps.text: Write the arrow, its contrapositive, and the given fact — then compare the fact against the arrow's left side.

rules.rule_text: A brief exceeding the page limit will be rejected by the clerk.

rules.note: Valid to infer; the converse (Q → P) and inverse (¬P → ¬Q) are NOT.

rules.rule_text: The defendant's brief exceeds the page limit.
rules.note: This matches the antecedent — modus ponens territory.

steps.title: Fire the rule
steps.text: The fact satisfies the antecedent exactly, so the consequent follows with certainty: the clerk will reject the defendant's brief. Watch the standard traps in the choices: the converse (treating the consequent as proof of the antecedent), the inverse (denying the antecedent), and out-of-scope add-ons the stimulus never mentions.

steps.title: Match the conclusion
steps.text: D is the modus ponens conclusion. A is the converse (rejection proves an oversized brief), B is the inverse, C wrongly claims indeterminacy, and E imports formatting facts from nowhere.

items.method: Symbolize the rule, then fire modus ponens

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A 'properly concluded' question over one conditional and one fact. The only valid moves are modus ponens (the fact matches the antecedent) and modus tollens (the fact negates the consequent) — symbolize and check which applies.

steps.title: Translate the rule and the fact
steps.text: Write the arrow, its contrapositive, and the given fact — then compare the fact against the arrow's left side.

rules.rule_text: Failing to record within thirty days costs the buyer's claim its priority.

rules.note: Valid to infer; the converse (Q → P) and inverse (¬P → ¬Q) are NOT.

rules.rule_text: Ms. Alvarez's title company failed to record within thirty days.
rules.note: This matches the antecedent — modus ponens territory.

steps.title: Fire the rule
steps.text: The fact satisfies the antecedent exactly, so the consequent follows with certainty: Ms. Alvarez's claim loses priority over later recorded claims. Watch the standard traps in the choices: the converse (treating the consequent as proof of the antecedent), the inverse (denying the antecedent), and out-of-scope add-ons the stimulus never mentions.

steps.title: Match the conclusion
steps.text: A is the modus ponens conclusion. B is the converse (assuming late recording is the only route to lost priority), C is the inverse dressed up as a guarantee, D wrongly claims indeterminacy, and E invents a damages entitlement the stimulus never grants.

items.method: Symbolize the rule, then fire modus ponens

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: A 'properly concluded' question over one conditional and one fact. The only valid moves are modus ponens (the fact matches the antecedent) and modus tollens (the fact negates the consequent) — symbolize and check which applies.

steps.title: Translate the rule and the fact
steps.text: Write the arrow, its contrapositive, and the given fact — then compare the fact against the arrow's left side.

rules.rule_text: Disclosing a trade secret to a competitor breaches the confidentiality agreement.

rules.note: Valid to infer; the converse (Q → P) and inverse (¬P → ¬Q) are NOT.

rules.rule_text: Deshawn disclosed a trade secret to a competitor.
rules.note: This matches the antecedent — modus ponens territory.

steps.title: Fire the rule
steps.text: The fact satisfies the antecedent exactly, so the consequent follows with certainty: Deshawn breached the confidentiality agreement. Watch the standard traps in the choices: the converse (treating the consequent as proof of the antecedent), the inverse (denying the antecedent), and out-of-scope add-ons the stimulus never mentions.

steps.title: Match the conclusion
steps.text: E is the modus ponens conclusion. A is the converse (breach proves disclosure), B is the inverse, C wrongly claims the matter cannot be determined, and D predicts termination — an outcome the stimulus never addresses.

items.method: Read tone from the hedges, not the topic

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: An author-attitude question. Attitude lives in evaluative language — concessions, hedges, worry words — not in the subject matter. Collect the author's actual verbs about Twombly and Iqbal before rating the temperature.

steps.title: Locate the attitude paragraph
steps.text: Your structure map says the modern cases live in the final paragraph — that's where the author's stance shows.

paragraphs.gist: Presents defenders' rationale (unforeseen discovery abuses) AND critics' fear ('risk reintroducing the very access barrier…'), with the author airing both.

steps.title: Weigh the hedges
steps.text: The author grants the cases responded to real problems, yet chooses loaded framing for the downside — 'risk reintroducing the very access barrier the 1938 drafters set out to dismantle.' That is neither cheerleading nor hostility: it's a measured worry with concessions attached. Calibrate the temperature: moderate, negative-leaning, hedged.

steps.title: Match the temperature
steps.text: C — qualified concern — matches a concession-plus-worry stance. A and B are the extremes the hedging rules out, D is contradicted by the author caring enough to flag the risk, and E invents confusion the passage never displays.

items.method: Attribute the view to the right speaker

steps.title: Name the task
steps.text: An inference question about what DEFENDERS of the cases believe — not the author, not the critics. Misattribution is the trap: find the one sentence the passage puts in the defenders' mouths and stay inside it.

steps.title: Locate the defenders' sentence
steps.text: Paragraph 4 assigns each camp exactly one position — keep them separate on your map.

paragraphs.gist: Defenders: mass-tort and antitrust complaints created discovery abuses the 1938 drafters could not have foreseen. Critics: the new standard risks restoring the old access barrier.

steps.title: Paraphrase the defenders' logic
steps.text: Their point: litigation changed after 1938 in ways that produced abuse, so the old permissive standard no longer fits — newer conditions justify a tougher threshold. The right answer will restate that modest claim; wrong answers will overshoot it (abolish notice pleading, condemn Conley) or smuggle in claims about litigants the defenders never made.

steps.title: Match the inference
steps.text: D — changes in litigation since 1938 justify a more demanding pleading standard — is the direct paraphrase. A and C overshoot into abolition and retroactive error, B smears pro se litigants without textual basis, and E resurrects the Field Code, which nobody in paragraph 4 endorses.
